source.title: Beyond Linearity in Attention Projections: The Case for Nonlinear Queries

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation loss for a parameter-matched architectural change and widened-model controls. This bears on the claim that architecture details matter little, and provides only a narrow, local comparison relevant to parameter scaling; it does not reproduce a scaling-law sweep.
record.gate_note: The study reports validation losses for a baseline, MLP-widened controls, and nonlinear-query models. The widened controls are a local parameter-count comparison, not a fitted power law. The authors' broader scaling-law predictions and cited results are not independent scaling-law tests.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper. It compares one parameter-neutral query modification (Residual GELU) against a NanoGPT baseline and MLP-widened controls at a single ~124M scale. Scaling laws serve only as a yardstick: it inverts a local Chinchilla-style exponent fitted to one control point to say the gain exceeds what more parameters would buy. No power-law sweep, extrapolation, allocation, or downstream result is produced. The query change is a new component, not the depth/width/aspect-ratio 'shape' variation V4 refers to, so it does not test V4. A single +12.5% width point cannot show a power law over orders of magnitude (V1).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the residual nonlinear query achieves 2.40% lower validation log-loss at the same parameter budget, beating a model with 12.5% more non-embedding parameters. They say this gain exceeds scaling-law predictions for the equivalent parameter increase and that the modification also tolerates LR/WD settings where the baseline diverges. They argue the algebraic redundancy of linear W_Q gives a structural reason to expect persistence at scale, and name testing at larger scale as the priority.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architectural comparison at one model scale, not a scaling-law sweep or fit across model sizes, data, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported losses differ across weight-decay and peak-learning-rate configurations; the authors state that lower weight decay requires a lower peak learning rate and that the baseline diverges at weight decay 0.05.

fits_no_version.finding: A nearly parameter-neutral nonlinear query projection lowers 124M validation loss by 2.40%. By the authors' local exponent, that equals ~35% more non-embedding parameters, versus 0.94% for +12.5% MLP width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural changes beyond shape can shift the loss-vs-parameters curve (an effective-parameter multiplier) at fixed parameter count.

record.peer_reviewed: arXiv preprint; the text says an earlier version appeared at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Geometry-grounded Representation Learning and Generative Modeling and a substantial part was accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries.
record.problems: Only one model scale is tested; there is no systematic hyperparameter search, no multiple-seed runs, and no uncertainty estimates. The study does not test scaling over orders of magnitude or compute-optimal allocation. Downstream evaluation is not reported.

untested.parts: No sweep over parameters, tokens or compute; only one local +12.5% width point at one scale.
No small-run fit used to predict larger runs.
No variation of depth, width, heads or aspect ratio at fixed parameter count.
No downstream evaluation; downstream predictability only cited from Gadre et al. and Xia et al.
No comparison of fits, parameter-count conventions or schedules.

missing.what: Additional MLP-widened controls (4.33d, 4.5d, 4.625d; 89.6–95.6M non-embedding parameters) appear as relative-loss curves. They could give a small local loss-vs-parameters trend but have no rows.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'reversed' on V4 conflates a new architectural component with Kaplan-style shape invariance. Even if counted, a 2.4% loss change is comparable to the few-percent shape effects Kaplan reports. The single control is about 0.9% lower loss for 1.125× parameters, close to what Kaplan's N-exponent would give. That is one point and is not evidence of a power law. Hyperparameters differ between the main runs and the baseline (higher LR, chosen from a sweep); there is one seed and no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Only a local parameter-count comparison is reported at the ∼124M scale. The study does not test power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude, token-count or compute scaling, or whether other quantities are non-bottlenecks.
No power laws fitted on small runs are used to predict and evaluate substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
Only one model scale and one principal architecture change are tested; the study does not explore a wide range of depths, widths, or other architecture details.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer setting is tested.
The authors report no downstream evaluation; downstream predictability is only discussed by reference to other work.
The study does not compare scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, data, or training schedules.

relation.reason: Section 3 inverts a local exponent calibrated to the widened control to estimate approximately 35% equivalent parameter growth; larger-scale validation remains future work.

tranche.reason: The study reports its architectural method's performance at one model scale and uses scaling laws to estimate an equivalent parameter increase. It does not test any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The six rows accurately reproduce method and control results, rather than results testing a claim version. Multiple seeds were not run; nonlinear variants use different learning-rate schedules, and the best result is selected from a sweep.
